title: PUC2-Sub Case 2a: Phishing Attack Training Scenario
description: Staff members undergo comprehensive hands-on training in identifying and reporting phishing campaigns through LMS theory modules, simulated email attacks via GoPhish, and automated scoring with personalised feedback. The training follows the PUC2 UML sequence: Training Setup → Trainee Executes Scenario → Assessment & Feedback.
outcomes: Identify phishing indicators in email headers, sender addresses, and body content
Detect social engineering tactics such as urgency, authority impersonation, and URL masking
Safely inspect attachments and embedded links without triggering tracking or executing malware
Apply organisational reporting protocols using the GoPhish platform and the REP incident form
Navigate the CyberRange platform tools: LMS portal, Mailpit inbox, GoPhish, and Grafana
Interpret automated scoring and personalised feedback to identify areas for improvement

levels.title: Welcome to Phishing Attack Training
levels.content:
## Welcome to PUC2-Sub Case 2a: Phishing Attack Training

In this training you will complete **30 levels** across three phases that mirror the UML sequence diagram for this scenario:

**Phase 1 — Training Setup** (Levels 1–9): Access and complete theory modules on the LMS portal, covering sender analysis, content red flags, and attachment verification.

**Phase 2 — Trainee Executes Scenario** (Levels 10–19): Receive and analyse a simulated phishing email delivered to your lab inbox. Identify indicators and submit a detection report.

**Phase 3 — Assessment and Feedback** (Levels 20–29): Complete a full email analysis, receive automated scoring and personalised feedback, and review cohort metrics in Grafana.

**Your platform tools — all accessible from your workstation browser:**
- LMS Portal: `http://lms.internal:8080/`
- Lab Email Inbox (Mailpit): `http://mail-relay.internal:8025/`
- Phishing Landing Page: `http://phishing-simulator.internal/`
- Reporting Dashboard (Grafana): `http://reporting.internal:3000/`

Connect to your Windows workstation and proceed to Level 1.

levels.title: Connect to Your Trainee Workstation
levels.cloud_content:

Once you can see the Windows desktop, open a browser and verify you can reach `http://lms.internal:8080/`. Then enter the passkey below to continue.

levels.title: Phase 1 — Training Setup
levels.content:
## Phase 1: Training Setup

The Training Instructor has published self-paced phishing awareness courses on the LMS portal. A GoPhish simulation campaign has been configured and is ready to deliver phishing emails to your lab inbox.

In this phase you will:
1. Open the LMS at `http://lms.internal:8080/` and review the course overview.
2. Complete theory Modules 1, 2 and 3.
3. Answer knowledge-check assessments after each module.

Take your time with each module — the indicators you learn here are exactly what you will need to identify in the live phishing email in Phase 2.

levels.title: LMS Portal — Assessment Scoring Overview
levels.content:
Open the LMS portal on your workstation: `http://lms.internal:8080/`

Navigate to the **Overview** tab and find the **Assessment Scoring** section. It lists the scoring components used to evaluate your performance in this training.

**Task:** How many scoring components are listed in the Assessment Scoring grid? Submit the number.
levels.solution:
The Assessment Scoring section on the Overview tab shows a 2×2 grid with four components:
1. Detection accuracy (40%)
2. Incident report completeness (30%)
3. Time to detection and report (20%)
4. Bonus: did NOT click the phishing link (+10%)

The correct answer is: **4**

hints.title: Where to look
hints.content: Scroll down on the Overview tab of the LMS. Look for a grid labelled 'Assessment Scoring'.

levels.title: Module 1 — Identify the Typosquatting Technique
levels.content:
In the LMS at `http://lms.internal:8080/`, navigate to **Module 1 — Sender Analysis**.

Read the section **Domain Look-alikes**. It describes a technique where attackers register domains that visually resemble legitimate ones — for example by substituting the digit zero for the letter O, or adding an extra word.

**Task:** What is the technical name of this domain impersonation technique? Submit the term in lowercase (one word).
levels.solution:
The technique is called **typosquatting** (also known as URL hijacking). Attackers register domains like `c0mpany.com` (zero instead of o) or `company-security.com` to deceive recipients.

The correct answer is: **typosquatting**

hints.title: Subsection name
hints.content: The technique is described under 'Domain Look-alikes' in Module 1. The word contains 'squatting'.

levels.title: Check — Email Header Concepts

questions.text: Which email header field is most commonly spoofed to display a trusted name?
Which mechanism validates that an email was sent from an authorised server for a domain?
An email shows From: it@company.com but Reply-To: it@helpdesk.xyz. What do you do?

choices.text: Report as suspicious — Reply-To mismatch is a red flag
Reply to the email to verify the sender
Forward to colleagues as a warning

questions.text: What does DKIM stand for? (write in full)

levels.instructions: Answer the following questions about email headers and sender authentication mechanisms.

levels.title: Module 2 — Count Urgency Tactic Examples
levels.content:
In the LMS at `http://lms.internal:8080/`, navigate to **Module 2 — Content Red Flags**.

Open the **Urgency and Fear Tactics** section. It includes a bulleted list of example phrases attackers use to pressure victims into acting immediately.

**Task:** How many distinct example phrases are listed as bullet points in that section? Submit the number.
levels.solution:
The Urgency and Fear Tactics section lists three bulleted example phrases:
1. 'Your account will be suspended within 24 hours'
2. 'Immediate action required — failure to respond will result in…'
3. 'URGENT: Verify your identity now'

The correct answer is: **3**

hints.title: Where to look
hints.content: Scroll to 'Urgency and Fear Tactics' in Module 2 and count the items in the bullet list of example phrases.

levels.title: Check — Malicious URLs and Social Engineering

questions.text: In the URL http://paypal.com.verify-login.evil.com/secure — which is the actual domain?
Which technique uses similar-looking Unicode characters to mimic a legitimate domain?
What social engineering principle is used in: 'Your CEO urgently requests you transfer €5,000 now'?

levels.instructions: Test your knowledge on URL analysis and social engineering principles.

levels.title: Module 3 — Identify a Dangerous Script Extension
levels.content:
In the LMS at `http://lms.internal:8080/`, navigate to **Module 3 — Attachments & Reporting**.

Read the **Attachment Red Flags** section. It lists categories of dangerous file types under **Executable files**.

**Task:** Which file extension listed under 'Executable files' is associated with PowerShell scripts? Include the dot (e.g. `.ext`).
levels.solution:
The Module 3 Executable files list includes `.exe`, `.bat`, `.ps1`, `.vbs`, and `.js`. The PowerShell script extension is `.ps1`.

The correct answer is: **.ps1**

hints.title: Executable files category
hints.content: In Module 3 under 'Attachment Red Flags', look at the 'Executable files' bullet. PowerShell files use a 3-letter extension.

levels.title: Check — Attachment Security

questions.text: Which file type is most commonly used to deliver malware via phishing emails?
A PDF attachment opens and immediately prompts 'Enable Content'. What should you do?

choices.text: Do NOT enable content — close and report as suspicious
Enable content to view the document
Save and re-open in a different viewer
Forward to IT with the file attached

questions.text: What is the safest way to verify whether a file sent by email is legitimate?

choices.text: Contact the sender via a separate, known communication channel
Reply to the email asking whether the file is safe
Open it on a personal device first
Scan with a free online antivirus tool

questions.text: What term describes malicious code embedded in Office macros that executes when the user enables them?

levels.instructions: Test your knowledge about dangerous attachment types and safe handling procedures.

levels.title: Phase 2 — Trainee Executes Scenario
levels.content:
## Phase 2: Trainee Executes Scenario

The GoPhish simulation campaign has delivered a phishing email to your lab inbox. You will now practise the skills you learned in Phase 1 against a real simulated attack.

In this phase you will:
1. Open your **Mailpit inbox** at `http://mail-relay.internal:8025/` and examine the phishing email.
2. Analyse the sender, subject, body, links, and attachments.
3. Use the **LMS Practical Exercise** form to submit your detection report.

**Important:** GoPhish tracks your actions. If you click the embedded phishing link, this will be recorded and will affect your score. The no-click bonus (10 pts) is only awarded if you do NOT click the link.

Proceed to the next level to begin your analysis.

levels.title: Mailpit — Check Your Lab Inbox
levels.content:
Open your lab email inbox on your workstation browser:

`http://mail-relay.internal:8025/`

Mailpit is a sandboxed email relay used in this lab. No emails leave the internal network. The GoPhish campaign has dispatched the simulated phishing email to your inbox.

**Task:** How many emails are currently in your inbox? Submit the number.
levels.solution:
The GoPhish campaign delivers exactly one phishing email per trainee. Your inbox should contain one unread message.

The correct answer is: **1**

hints.title: Mailpit interface
hints.content: The Mailpit web UI shows a list of messages at http://mail-relay.internal:8025/. Count the messages in the inbox list.

levels.title: Mailpit — Analyse the Sender Domain TLD
levels.content:
Open the phishing email in your Mailpit inbox at `http://mail-relay.internal:8025/`.

Carefully examine the **From** field. There are two parts: the *display name* (the friendly name shown) and the *actual email address* in angle brackets `< >`.

Attackers use a legitimate-looking display name but a spoofed domain. The spoofed sender in this simulation uses a top-level domain (TLD) that differs from the organisation’s real `.com` domain.

**Task:** What is the TLD of the sender’s actual email address (the part after the last dot)? Submit only the TLD without the dot (e.g. if the TLD were `.org`, submit `org`).
levels.solution:
Look past the display name to the actual address in angle brackets. The phishing email is sent from a domain ending in **.net** (e.g. `security@company-corp.net`) instead of the legitimate `.com` domain.

This TLD substitution is a classic typosquatting/domain spoofing technique.

The correct answer is: **net**

hints.title: Display name vs. real address
hints.content: In Mailpit, click the email and look at the raw From field. The display name may say 'IT Security Team' but the address in < > uses a different domain.

hints.title: TLD mismatch
hints.content: The real company uses .com. The spoofed address uses a different TLD. Check the last segment of the domain after the final dot.

levels.title: Mailpit — Identify the Email Body Heading
levels.content:
Still viewing the phishing email in Mailpit at `http://mail-relay.internal:8025/`.

Open the email and look at the **main heading** at the top of the email body (the bold red banner text). Phishing emails commonly use a prominent urgency keyword in their heading to trigger an immediate emotional response before the recipient thinks critically.

**Task:** What is the **first alphabetic word** of the email body heading? (Ignore any symbols or icons — submit the first actual word in uppercase.)
levels.solution:
The phishing email body heading reads:

**⚠ URGENT: IT Security Compliance Action Required**

Ignoring the warning symbol, the first alphabetic word is **URGENT**.

This deliberate capitalisation is a social engineering tactic designed to create panic and bypass rational evaluation.

The correct answer is: **URGENT**

hints.title: Where to look
hints.content: Look at the bold red banner/heading at the top of the rendered email body in Mailpit — not the Subject line in the inbox list.

levels.title: Mailpit — Inspect the GoPhish Tracking Parameter
levels.content:
In Mailpit, open the phishing email. Find the **‘Verify Compliance Now’** call-to-action button or link.

**Do NOT click the link.** Instead, right-click it and select **Copy Link Address** (or hover to see the URL in your browser status bar).

GoPhish appends a unique tracking query parameter to every campaign link so it can record which recipient clicked. This parameter is the same for all GoPhish campaigns.

**Task:** What is the **name** of the query parameter appended by GoPhish to the link URL? (e.g. for `http://site.com/?param=abc`, the parameter name is `param`). Submit only the parameter name.
levels.solution:
GoPhish appends `?rid=<unique_recipient_id>` to all campaign phishing links. The parameter name is **rid** (Recipient ID).

Example full URL: `http://phishing-simulator.internal/?rid=Ab3xYz9`

This allows GoPhish to associate each click with a specific target in the campaign results.

The correct answer is: **rid**

hints.title: Copy without clicking
hints.content: Right-click the link in the email and select 'Copy Link Address'. Paste it into a text editor to read it safely.

hints.title: Query parameter format
hints.content: A URL query string starts with ? followed by key=value pairs. In GoPhish the key is a 3-letter word related to 'recipient'.

levels.title: Mailpit — Count Urgency Phrases in the Email Body
levels.content:
Read the full body of the phishing email in Mailpit carefully.

Count each **distinct urgency or fear trigger** present. Examples of triggers to look for:
- Words/phrases conveying time pressure: *immediately*, *within 24 hours*, *expires*, *urgent*
- Threats or negative consequences: *suspended*, *account locked*, *deletion*, *action required*
- Compliance-based pressure: *policy violation*, *overdue*, *pending re-verification*

Count each distinct trigger once (do not count the same phrase twice if it repeats).

**Task:** How many distinct urgency or fear trigger phrases are present in the email body and heading? Submit the number.
levels.solution:
The phishing email 'IT Security Compliance Notice' contains four distinct urgency/fear triggers:
1. **URGENT** — in the email heading
2. **immediate verification** — in the first paragraph
3. **within 24 hours** — deadline pressure
4. **temporary account suspension** — threat of consequence

The correct answer is: **4**

hints.title: Where to look
hints.content: Check both the heading (URGENT:...) and the body paragraph. Look for time pressure words and threat phrases.

hints.title: Triggers list
hints.content: Look for: URGENT, immediate, 24 hours, suspended/suspension, overdue, pending, action required.

levels.title: Check — Content Red Flags

questions.text: An email states: 'URGENT: Your account will be permanently deleted in 24 HOURS unless you verify NOW.' Which social engineering tactic is predominantly used?

choices.text: Urgency and fear — manufactured time pressure with a threat
Social proof — claiming others have already acted

questions.text: A phishing email is addressed to 'Dear Valued Employee' instead of your full name. What does this indicate about the attack?

choices.text: It is likely a mass-targeted campaign — the attacker does not have personalised details
The sender uses a formal email style
The email was auto-forwarded and stripped the recipient name
The sender’s email client does not support personalisation

questions.text: A link in an email displays 'https://company.com/login' but hovering reveals 'http://phishing-simulator.internal/?rid=abc'. What is this technique called?

choices.text: URL masking — the visible anchor text differs from the actual href target

levels.instructions: Test your knowledge about email content red flags and social engineering tactics.

levels.title: Mailpit — Find the Security Policy Reference
levels.content:
Read the **body** of the phishing email in Mailpit carefully.

Attackers often include fake policy or reference codes to make phishing emails appear official and authoritative. These manufactured codes exploit the victim’s fear of non-compliance with internal regulations.

**Task:** Find the internal security policy code mentioned in the email body (format: `XXX-YYYY-NN`). Submit it exactly as it appears.
levels.solution:
The phishing email body contains the sentence:

*’…in accordance with policy **SEC-2024-11**.’*

This fictitious policy reference is included to make the email appear to originate from a legitimate compliance system and to pressure the recipient into acting without questioning.

The correct answer is: **SEC-2024-11**

hints.title: Where to look
hints.content: Read the second paragraph of the email body. Look for a policy code in the format XXX-YYYY-NN.

levels.title: LMS — Submit Your Detection Report
levels.content:
Navigate to the LMS at `http://lms.internal:8080/` and open the **Practical Exercise** tab.

Fill in the detection report form:
1. Enter your name or trainee ID.
2. Mark the email as **suspicious**.
3. List **at least three red flags** you identified (one per line). Be specific: mention sender domain, urgency language, malicious URL, attachment extension, etc.
4. Indicate whether you clicked the phishing link.
5. Click **Submit Detection Report**.

After submission, a confirmation message appears. It contains a link to a cohort metrics dashboard.

**Task:** What is the **hostname** of the reporting system linked in the confirmation message? (e.g. `hostname.internal`)
levels.solution:
After submitting the report, the confirmation box shows:

*'Your personalised feedback will arrive in your lab inbox… Cohort results: Grafana Dashboard →'*

The Grafana dashboard link points to `http://reporting.internal:3000/`. The hostname is **reporting.internal**.

The correct answer is: **reporting.internal**

hints.title: Confirmation message
hints.content: After clicking 'Submit Detection Report', a yellow confirmation box appears. Look for a URL link to a dashboard.

hints.title: Reporting system
hints.content: The linked dashboard is Grafana. Its hostname follows the pattern: service.internal

levels.title: LMS — Verify Sender Identity via Corporate Directory
levels.content:
Open the LMS module at `http://lms.internal:8080/module2/`. This page simulates a corporate staff directory that you can use to verify email senders.

Look up the claimed sender of the phishing email (the person or team it pretends to be from). Compare the **email domain** of the sender’s entry in the directory with the **From domain** of the phishing email you received in Mailpit.

**Task:** Do the domains MATCH or MISMATCH? Submit `MATCH` or `MISMATCH` in uppercase.
levels.solution:
The corporate directory lists the legitimate IT Security team address as ending in `.com` (e.g. `company-corp.com`), while the phishing email's From address uses `.net` (e.g. `company-corp.net`).

The domains are different — this is a classic sender spoofing indicator.

The correct answer is: **MISMATCH**

hints.title: What to compare
hints.content: Compare the domain part (after the @) of the phishing email's From address with the domain shown in the directory for the same contact.

levels.title: Phase 3 — Assessment and Feedback
levels.content:
## Phase 3: Assessment and Feedback

You have completed the practical exercises. Well done.

In this phase the platform will:
- **Score** your actions against the learning objectives (Step 6 of the UML)
- **Deliver personalised feedback** to your Mailpit inbox (Step 7)
- **Report cohort metrics** to the instructor via Grafana (Step 8)

Your composite score is calculated from:
| Component | Points |
|---|---|
| Detection accuracy (reported the email) | 40 |
| Report completeness (incident form submitted) | 30 |
| Time to report | 20 |
| No-click bonus (did not click the link) | 10 |

**Timing note:** The instructor will run `SCORE_CAMPAIGN` and `DELIVER_FEEDBACK` once all trainees have submitted their detection reports (Level 18). When you reach Level 23, if your feedback email has not yet arrived in Mailpit, wait 2–3 minutes and refresh before proceeding.

Proceed through the remaining levels to review your results.

levels.title: Full Email Analysis — Count Indicator Categories
levels.content:
Conduct a **comprehensive analysis** of the phishing email you received. Review it in Mailpit at `http://mail-relay.internal:8025/` and systematically check:

1. **Sender domain** — does it match the legitimate organisation?
2. **Reply-To header** — does it match the From domain?
3. **Embedded links** — do they point to the expected domain?
4. **Body language** — urgency, threats, or fear tactics?
5. **Greeting** — is it personalised or generic?

Count the number of **distinct phishing indicator categories** present in the email (one count per category, regardless of how many instances of each you find).

**Task:** How many distinct indicator categories did you identify? Submit the number.
levels.solution:
A thorough analysis of the phishing email reveals five distinct indicator categories:
1. **Spoofed sender domain** — From uses `.net` instead of legitimate `.com`
2. **Reply-To mismatch** — Reply-To domain differs from From domain
3. **Malicious embedded URL** — link points to phishing-simulator.internal
4. **Urgency and fear language** — URGENT, immediate, 24 hours, suspension
5. **Generic greeting** — 'Dear Valued Employee' rather than the recipient’s name

The correct answer is: **5**

hints.title: Systematic checklist
hints.content: Check five categories in order: (1) From domain, (2) Reply-To header, (3) hovering over links, (4) urgency language in body, (5) personalisation of the greeting.

hints.title: Counting rule
hints.content: Count each category once, even if multiple instances exist within it.

levels.title: Check — Sender Verification and Incident Reporting

questions.text: You suspect a phishing email has arrived. What is the CORRECT first action?

choices.text: Do not click any links — report to the security team immediately
Forward to colleagues to warn them
Reply to the sender asking whether it is legitimate

questions.text: Which is a valid reporting channel for a suspected phishing email?

choices.text: A 'Report Phishing' button or a dedicated security team email alias
Posting about it on internal social media
Calling the displayed sender phone number

questions.text: You accidentally clicked a suspicious link. What is the most important NEXT step?

choices.text: Disconnect from the network and contact IT security immediately
Close the browser tab and continue working
Run a full antivirus scan and reboot
Change your email password but do not report

questions.text: Name one specific piece of information that should always be included when reporting a phishing email.

levels.instructions: Test your knowledge on phishing incident handling and reporting procedures.

levels.title: Mailpit — Read Your Feedback Email
levels.content:
Open your Mailpit inbox at `http://mail-relay.internal:8025/` and find the feedback email sent by the training platform.

The subject will be:
**[Training Platform] Your Phishing Awareness Score — X/100**

If the email has not arrived yet, wait 2–3 minutes and refresh the page — the instructor runs the scoring engine after all trainees submit their detection reports.

Open the email. It contains your total score, a breakdown by component, a list of missed indicators, and module recommendations.

**Task:** Looking at the score breakdown table in the feedback email, what is the **maximum possible total score**? Submit the number.
levels.solution:
The feedback email shows a score breakdown table with four components:
- Detection Accuracy: max 40 pts
- Report Completeness: max 30 pts
- Time to Report: max 20 pts
- No-Click Bonus: max 10 pts

Total maximum: 40 + 30 + 20 + 10 = **100** points.

The correct answer is: **100**

hints.title: Score breakdown
hints.content: Add the maximum values shown for each scoring component in the breakdown table.

levels.title: LMS My Feedback — Identify the Lab Inbox Port
levels.content:
Navigate to the LMS at `http://lms.internal:8080/` and click the **My Feedback** tab in the navigation bar.

This tab shows where to find your personalised feedback and links to the lab email inbox.

**Task:** What is the **TCP port number** shown in the Mailpit inbox URL displayed on the My Feedback tab? Submit only the port number.
levels.solution:
The My Feedback tab displays the Mailpit inbox URL:
`http://mail-relay.internal:8025/`

The port number is **8025** (Mailpit’s default HTTP port for the WebUI).

The correct answer is: **8025**

hints.title: URL format
hints.content: In the URL http://hostname:PORT/, the port number follows the colon after the hostname.

levels.title: Grafana — Find the Score Component Averages Panel
levels.content:
Open the Grafana Reporting Workspace at `http://reporting.internal:3000/` in your workstation browser.

Navigate to the **REP Overview** dashboard (under the REP folder in the left sidebar, or browse dashboards).

The bottom section of the dashboard contains two table panels side by side. One shows per-trainee scores, the other shows cohort averages broken down by scoring component.

**Task:** What is the exact **title** of the table panel in the **bottom-right** that shows cohort average, max, and min for each scoring component? Submit the title exactly as it appears in the panel header.
levels.solution:
The bottom-right table panel is titled:

**Score Component Averages**

It shows one row per scoring component (Detection Accuracy, Report Completeness, Time to Report, No-Click Bonus) with columns for Avg, Max, and Min across all scored trainees.

The correct answer is: **Score Component Averages**

hints.title: Finding the dashboard
hints.content: In Grafana, click the compass/Browse icon, then look under the REP folder for the REP Overview dashboard.

hints.title: Which panel
hints.content: Look at the two table panels in the bottom half of the dashboard. The one on the right shows averages per component.

levels.title: Grafana — Find the Per-Trainee Scores Panel
levels.content:
Still in the Grafana REP Overview dashboard at `http://reporting.internal:3000/`.

The dashboard includes a table panel that lists every trainee with their traffic-light status (Detected / Partial / At Risk), total score, and individual component scores.

**Task:** What is the **exact title** of this per-trainee table panel? Submit it exactly as it appears in the panel header.
levels.solution:
The table panel that lists per-trainee scores with traffic-light status coloring is titled:

**Trainee Scores**

This panel queries the `trainee_scores` table in the REP PostgreSQL database and displays the `traffic_light`, `score_total`, and individual component scores per trainee.

The correct answer is: **Trainee Scores**

hints.title: Panel location
hints.content: The per-trainee table is the large panel in the middle section of the REP Overview dashboard, spanning the full width.

levels.title: Self-Assessment Questionnaire

questions.text: Before this training, how confident were you in identifying phishing emails?
After completing this training, how confident do you feel in identifying phishing emails?
Which topic was most challenging for you in this training?

choices.text: Spoofed sender domains and TLD analysis

questions.text: What was the single most valuable thing you learned in this training?

levels.title: Final Knowledge Test

questions.text: An email arrives from security@paypa1.com. What is the phishing indicator?

choices.text: The domain uses digit 1 instead of letter l — a lookalike (typosquatted) domain
The display name contains the word Security
The email was delivered via SMTP

questions.text: Which is a legitimate reason to click a link in an unsolicited email?

choices.text: None — always verify the sender and purpose before clicking any link
If the email is from a well-known company name
If the link starts with HTTPS
If you were expecting an email from that sender

questions.text: What does DMARC protect against?

choices.text: Email domain spoofing — it specifies how servers handle authentication failures

questions.text: An email has: mismatched From/Reply-To, urgency language, a generic greeting, and a .ru link. How many phishing indicator categories is that?
Which technique sends targeted phishing emails that include personalised details about the victim?
An email attachment is named Q1_Report.xlsx.js. What is the real file type?

choices.text: JavaScript (.js) — the .xlsx is a decoy extension

questions.text: You clicked a suspicious link in an email. What is the MOST important immediate action?

choices.text: Disconnect from the network and contact the security team
Run Windows Defender and then reboot
Check whether the site looked legitimate before deciding

questions.text: 'Only 3 spots remaining — register NOW before they’re gone!' Which social engineering principle does this exploit?

choices.text: Scarcity — artificially limiting availability to create urgency
Authority — impersonating a figure of power
Reciprocity — offering something to create obligation
Social proof — referencing the behaviour of others

questions.text: Which email authentication protocol uses DNS TXT records to specify which mail servers are authorised to send on behalf of a domain? (submit the acronym)
Which best describes a Business Email Compromise (BEC) attack?

choices.text: Impersonating an executive or trusted vendor to trick employees into transferring funds or data
Breaking into the company email server by exploiting a vulnerability
A denial-of-service attack targeting the mail server
Phishing carried out via SMS messages

levels.instructions: This is the final graded test covering all topics from the training. Each question is worth 10 points for a maximum of 100 points.

levels.title: Training Complete — Next Steps
levels.content:
## Congratulations — Training Complete!

You have successfully completed all 30 levels of the **PUC2-Sub Case 2a: Phishing Attack Training Scenario**.

### Key takeaways
- **Always check the real sender address**, not just the display name
- **Hover before you click** — visible link text can differ from the actual URL
- **Urgency is a red flag** — pause and verify before acting
- **Real file extensions matter** — enable 'show extensions' in Windows
- **Report, don’t react** — use the report button or security team alias
- **Time matters** — fast detection limits attacker dwell time

### Next steps
